body.heading: The three-purchase trap
paragraphs: A $25 umbrella that collapses in the first storm, replaced twice, costs $75 and three soakings. A $60 umbrella that lasts five winters costs $60 and none. Cheap is a price; inexpensive is a cost over time, and the two part company quickly.

This applies beyond objects. A slightly dearer train ticket at a civilised hour can save a taxi, a missed connection, and a ruined day. Total cost includes your time and trouble, not just the receipt.

body.heading: Signs the dearer option earns it
paragraphs: Look for evidence, not adjectives: a long guarantee, replaceable parts, a repair service, solid materials, and reviews mentioning years of use. "Premium" printed on a box is marketing; a ten-year warranty is a commitment.
Repairability is the strongest signal of all. Things designed to be opened, fixed, and fitted with new parts are things designed to be kept.

body.heading: And when it does not
paragraphs: Paying more only pays back when you will use the thing long enough to collect. For short-lived needs, fashion experiments, and growing children, the cheap or borrowed option remains the wise one. Match the spending to the lifespan of the need.

A middle path often exists: the mid-priced, repairable version, or the quality item bought second-hand. Cost over a whole life, not the drama of the highest price, is the measure — and it frequently lands in the middle.

takeaway: Before choosing the cheapest, ask what it costs over its whole life — repairs, replacements, and your time included. Sometimes the honest bargain is the dearer one.
